questions.stem: The term "textiles" originally referred to
questions.explanation: From Latin texere, to weave; it now covers all fibres, yarns and fabrics.

questions.stem: Which of the following careers is directly related to textiles?
questions.explanation: Fabric designers, dyers, weavers and textile technologists work in textiles.

questions.stem: Aso oke, worn at Yoruba ceremonies, is an example of how textiles express
questions.explanation: Traditional fabrics carry cultural meaning, prestige and identity.

questions.stem: Akwete cloth, woven by women on a broad upright loom, is associated with
questions.explanation: Akwete weaving is a women's craft of Akwete in Abia State.

questions.stem: Silk is obtained from
options: the seed hairs of a plant
questions.explanation: Silk is a protein filament spun by the silkworm.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a synthetic fibre?
questions.explanation: Polyester is made from petrochemicals.

questions.stem: Flax (linen) is classified as a
questions.explanation: Flax fibres come from the stem (bast) of the plant.

questions.stem: A fibre that burns slowly with a smell like burning hair and leaves a crushable black ash is
questions.explanation: Protein fibres smell of burning hair; cotton smells of burning paper; synthetics melt.

questions.stem: The process of separating cotton fibres from the seeds is called
questions.explanation: Ginning removes seeds; retting rots flax stems to free fibres.

questions.stem: Soaking flax stalks in water so that bacteria loosen the fibres from the woody stem is
questions.explanation: Retting breaks down pectin binding the fibres.

questions.stem: Viscose rayon is described as a regenerated fibre because it is
options: made from natural cellulose (wood pulp) that is chemically processed and re-formed
questions.explanation: Regenerated fibres re-form natural polymers; synthetics are built from petrochemicals.

questions.stem: A yarn made by twisting two single yarns together is a
questions.explanation: Plying twists singles together for strength and evenness.

questions.stem: A fabric whose fibres are combined, such as polyester and cotton spun together in one yarn, is a
options: mixture of separate warp and weft yarns
questions.explanation: In a blend fibres are mixed before spinning; in a mixture different yarns are used in warp and weft.

questions.stem: In weaving, the threads that run lengthwise on the loom are the
questions.explanation: Warp is lengthwise; weft crosses it.

questions.stem: A weave in which each weft passes over one warp and under the next is
questions.explanation: Plain weave is the simplest over-one-under-one interlacing.

questions.stem: Denim and drill are recognised by diagonal lines on the surface, showing that they are
questions.explanation: Twill produces diagonal wales.

questions.stem: The weave with long warp floats on the face, giving a smooth lustrous surface, is
questions.explanation: Satin is warp-faced; sateen is weft-faced.

questions.stem: Shedding, picking and beating-up are known as the
questions.explanation: Primary motions form the shed, insert the weft and beat it in.

questions.stem: Threading the warp ends through the eyes of the heddles is called
questions.explanation: Heddling sets the order for shedding; reeding passes ends through the reed dents.

questions.stem: A warp 50 cm wide is set at 20 ends per cm. If each warp end is 3 m long, the total length of warp yarn required is
Knitting differs from weaving because knitted fabric is made by
options: interlacing warp and weft at right angles
pressing fibres with heat and moisture
questions.explanation: Knitting forms loops; weaving interlaces two sets of yarn.

questions.stem: Felt is an example of a
options: non-woven fabric made by matting fibres with heat, moisture and pressure
questions.explanation: Wool fibres interlock under heat, moisture and agitation to form felt.

questions.stem: In weaving, the reed performs the function of
options: spacing the warp ends and beating the weft into place
carrying the weft across the shed
questions.explanation: The reed beats up each pick and keeps ends evenly spaced; the shuttle carries the weft.

questions.stem: Batik is a method of decorating fabric in which
options: threads are pulled out of the fabric
hot wax is used to resist the dye
a heated roller presses the cloth
questions.explanation: Waxed areas resist dye, forming the pattern.

questions.stem: The tool used to draw fine wax lines in batik is the
questions.explanation: The tjanting has a small reservoir and spout for wax.

questions.stem: Adire eleko is a Yoruba resist-dyed cloth in which the resist is
questions.explanation: Eleko uses starch paste applied freehand or through stencils before indigo dyeing.

questions.stem: A substance used to fix a dye permanently on fibres is a
questions.explanation: Mordants such as alum bind dyes to fibres.

questions.stem: In screen printing, dye paste is pushed through the open areas of the screen with a
questions.explanation: The squeegee draws paste across the mesh.

questions.stem: Cloth dyed in an indigo vat comes out greenish-yellow and turns blue on exposure to air because
options: water evaporates and leaves blue salt
the reduced dye is oxidised by air back to insoluble blue indigo
questions.explanation: Indigo is reduced to a soluble form in the vat and re-oxidised to blue on the fibre.

questions.stem: Treating cotton under tension with caustic soda to increase its lustre, strength and dye uptake is
questions.explanation: Mercerisation is a chemical finish named after John Mercer.

questions.stem: Passing fabric between heavy heated rollers to give it a smooth, glossy surface is
questions.explanation: Calendering is a mechanical finish.

questions.stem: Decorating fabric with ornamental stitches such as chain, satin and stem stitch is
questions.explanation: Embroidery uses decorative needlework stitches.

questions.stem: Which practice supports sustainable textile production?
options: Recycling fabric off-cuts into new products
questions.explanation: Recycling reduces waste and saves resources.

questions.stem: A healthy studio practice when mixing dyes and chemicals is to
options: wear gloves and work in a well-ventilated area
questions.explanation: PPE and ventilation reduce chemical exposure.

questions.stem: Using dyes from local plants such as indigo and camwood is encouraged for sustainability because they
options: are renewable and usually less harmful to the environment
questions.explanation: Natural dyes come from renewable sources with lower pollution.

questions.stem: A collection of an artist's best works, kept to show skills to clients or examiners, is a
questions.explanation: A portfolio showcases selected works, in hard or soft copy.

questions.stem: An exhibition of the works of only one textile artist is
questions.explanation: Solo = one artist; group = several artists.

questions.stem: A written document describing a business idea, its market, operations and finances is
questions.explanation: The business plan guides the enterprise and attracts funding.

questions.stem: A weaver spends ₦6,000 on yarn and ₦2,000 on other costs to make a stole and adds 25% profit on total cost. The selling price is
questions.explanation: Total cost = ₦8,000; 25% of 8,000 = ₦2,000; selling price = ₦10,000.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a good way of marketing textile products?
options: Displaying them at trade fairs and on social media
questions.explanation: Exhibitions and online platforms reach customers.

questions.stem:
(a) Classify textile fibres, giving two examples under each class. [6 marks]
(b) Describe how a burning test can be used to distinguish cotton, wool and nylon. [6 marks]
(c) State three properties that make cotton suitable for school uniforms. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: Natural vegetable/cellulose: cotton, flax, jute, sisal, raffia (any two)
2 marks: Natural animal/protein: wool, silk, mohair (any two)
2 marks: Man-made: regenerated (viscose, acetate) and synthetic (nylon, polyester, acrylic) - any two
2 marks: Cotton: burns quickly with yellow flame, smell of burning paper, soft grey ash
2 marks: Wool: burns slowly, self-extinguishes, smell of burning hair/feathers, crushable black ash
2 marks: Nylon: melts and shrinks from flame, drips, forms hard bead, chemical/celery-like smell
3 marks: Any three (1 each): absorbent and cool; strong, especially when wet; washable at high temperature; comfortable/does not irritate skin; takes dye well; cheap
questions.explanation: Fibres are natural (vegetable: cotton, flax; animal: wool, silk) or man-made (regenerated: viscose; synthetic: nylon, polyester). Burning test: cotton smells of paper and leaves grey ash; wool smells of hair with crushable ash; nylon melts into a hard bead. Cotton is absorbent, strong and washable.

questions.stem:
Describe the following processes in preparing a loom for weaving:
(a) warping; [3 marks]
(b) beaming; [3 marks]
(c) heddling (drawing-in); [3 marks]
(d) reeding (sleying); [3 marks]
(e) tying up. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: Warping: measuring and arranging the required number of warp ends to the correct length, in order and under even tension, on a warping board or mill
3 marks: Beaming: winding the warp evenly and under tension onto the warp beam of the loom
3 marks: Heddling: threading each warp end through the eye of a heddle on the correct shaft according to the draft
3 marks: Reeding: passing the ends through the dents of the reed in the required order to space them and set the width
3 marks: Tying up: tying the ends to the cloth beam (front apron rod) with even tension and connecting shafts to treadles/levers
questions.explanation: Warping measures the ends; beaming winds them onto the warp beam; heddling threads them through heddles; reeding passes them through the reed; tying up fastens them to the cloth beam and links shafts to treadles.

questions.stem:
(a) Describe plain, twill and satin weaves, stating one use of each. [9 marks]
(b) A fabric 2.5 m long has 16 picks per cm. The fabric is 50 cm wide. Calculate (i) the total number of picks; (ii) the total length of weft yarn used, ignoring take-up and waste. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: Plain: weft passes over one and under one warp alternately; firm, both sides alike; e.g. calico, shirting
3 marks: Twill: interlacing steps one end each pick forming diagonal lines; strong, durable; e.g. denim, drill, gabardine
3 marks: Satin: few interlacings with long warp floats on the face; smooth and lustrous; e.g. linings, evening wear
3 marks: Picks = 250 cm x 16 = 4,000 picks
3 marks: Weft length = 4,000 x 0.5 m = 2,000 m
questions.explanation: Plain is over-one-under-one; twill forms diagonal lines; satin has long floats. 250 cm x 16 picks/cm = 4,000 picks; each 0.5 m wide gives 2,000 m of weft.

questions.stem:
(a) List four materials needed for tie and dye. [4 marks]
(b) Describe the steps for producing a tie-dye fabric with a vat dye. [8 marks]
(c) State three safety precautions to observe during dyeing. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: Any four (1 each): white cotton fabric; dye (e.g. vat dye/indigo); caustic soda; sodium hydrosulphite; raffia/thread/rubber bands; basins; gloves; stirring rod; water
2 marks: Wash/desize the fabric to remove starch and dry it
2 marks: Tie, fold, stitch or clamp the fabric according to the design
2 marks: Prepare the dye bath (dye, caustic soda, hydrosulphite) and immerse wet fabric for the required time
2 marks: Remove, oxidise in air, rinse, untie, wash/rinse again, dry and iron
3 marks: Any three (1 each): wear gloves and apron; work in a ventilated area; keep chemicals labelled and away from food; avoid splashes to eyes; wash hands after work
questions.explanation: Tie-dye needs cotton, dye, caustic soda, hydrosulphite and ties. Steps: wash fabric, tie the design, dye in the reduced vat, oxidise, rinse, untie, wash and iron. Wear gloves, ventilate, label chemicals.

questions.stem:
(a) Distinguish between mechanical and chemical finishes, giving two examples of each. [6 marks]
(b) State three reasons why fabrics are finished. [3 marks]
(c) State three ways of caring for a printed cotton fabric. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: Mechanical finishes use physical/mechanical action: e.g. calendering, brushing/raising, sanforising, shearing (any two)
3 marks: Chemical finishes use chemicals: e.g. mercerising, bleaching, waterproofing, flame-proofing, crease-resistant finishing (any two)
3 marks: Any three (1 each): improve appearance; improve handle/feel; increase durability; give special properties (water repellence, shrink resistance); increase market value
6 marks: Any three (2 each): wash in mild soap and cool/warm water; avoid bleach; dry in shade inside out; iron on the reverse side at correct temperature; wash separately to avoid colour bleeding; store dry and folded
questions.explanation: Mechanical finishes (calendering, raising, sanforising) use physical action; chemical finishes (mercerising, bleaching, waterproofing) use chemicals. Finishes improve appearance, handle and durability. Care: mild soap, no bleach, dry in shade, iron on reverse.

questions.stem:
(a) State five key points that should be included in a business plan for a small textile enterprise. [5 marks]
(b) A batik maker uses materials worth ₦12,000 and labour and overheads of ₦6,000 to produce 6 wrappers. Calculate (i) the cost of one wrapper; (ii) the selling price of one wrapper if 30% profit is added on cost. [6 marks]
(c) State two ways of promoting indigenous textiles. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
5 marks: Any five (1 each): business name and description; objectives; products/services; market analysis and customers; marketing plan; location and equipment; staffing; financial plan/start-up capital; risk assessment
3 marks: Cost of one wrapper = (12,000 + 6,000) / 6 = ₦3,000
3 marks: Selling price = 3,000 + 30% of 3,000 = ₦3,900
4 marks: Any two (2 each): exhibitions and trade fairs; use in school/office uniforms and ceremonies; social media marketing; government patronage/policy; fashion shows
questions.explanation: A business plan covers the business description, products, market, marketing, location, staff and finance. Cost per wrapper = ₦18,000/6 = ₦3,000; with 30% profit selling price = ₦3,900. Promote via exhibitions, uniforms and social media.
